lessons.title: Detailed Notes: System Software
lessons.notes_html:
The importance of system software

System software is important because it is what makes a computer work at all: without it, the hardware is a collection of parts that cannot cooperate, and application software has nothing to run on. The operating system manages hardware resources (CPU, memory, storage, devices), provides the user interface through which people operate the machine, and runs and coordinates applications. Utility software keeps the system performing well and secure by cleaning disks, removing malware and maintaining files. Device drivers let the operating system communicate with each specific hardware device. In short, system software facilitates communication between hardware and software, manages resources efficiently, and creates the stable platform on which every user task — writing, calculating, designing, browsing — depends.

Operating systems, utilities and drivers: their roles

The operating system is the core system software: it manages hardware resources (deciding which program gets CPU time and memory), provides the user interface (windows, icons, menus), runs applications, and manages files; examples are Windows, macOS and Linux. Utility software enhances system performance, security and maintenance: Disk Cleanup frees space by removing temporary files, antivirus software detects and removes malware, disk defragmenters organize data for faster access, and backup utilities protect data; each keeps the system healthy rather than doing a user task. Device drivers are the translators between the operating system and hardware: a printer driver converts the operating system's print command into the exact instructions a particular printer model needs, a graphics driver lets the operating system use the graphics card's full capability, and a mouse driver interprets mouse movements; without the correct driver the device cannot communicate properly with the system.

System software and application software in detail

System software and application software differ in purpose, user interaction and dependence. Purpose: system software manages and runs the computer (operating systems, utilities, drivers), while application software performs specific tasks for the user (word processing, spreadsheets, presentations, graphic design). Interaction: the user rarely interacts directly with system software, which works in the background, whereas application software is used directly for visible work such as writing a document. Dependence: application software cannot run without system software — a word processor needs an operating system to reach the CPU, memory and printer — while system software can run without any particular application. Examples make the split clear: Windows and Disk Cleanup are system software; Microsoft Word and a spreadsheet program are application software. Both are needed, but they serve different layers of the computer.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes: Utilities, Drivers and Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Using utilities to optimize performance and security

Using utility software follows a regular maintenance routine. Step 1: clean up the disk with a tool such as Disk Cleanup, removing temporary files, recycle-bin contents and unused system files to free space. Step 2: check and repair the disk, scanning for file-system errors and bad sectors before they cause data loss. Step 3: defragment (on a traditional hard drive) so file fragments are reorganized and access becomes faster. Step 4: secure the system with antivirus software — update its definitions, run a full scan, and quarantine or remove any malware found. Step 5: manage start-up programs and uninstall unused applications, so the computer boots faster and fewer background programs consume resources. Step 6: back up important data with a backup utility to an external drive or cloud storage, and verify the backup can be restored. Step 7: keep the operating system and drivers updated, since updates fix bugs and security holes. Done regularly, this routine keeps the computer fast, stable and secure.

Installing, updating and troubleshooting device drivers

Install: when new hardware is connected, the operating system often installs a driver automatically; otherwise insert the manufacturer's disc or download the driver from the manufacturer's official website, run the installer, and restart if asked. Always use the driver for the exact device model and operating system version. Update: open the device manager, find the device, and choose to update its driver, or download the newest version from the manufacturer; updates fix bugs, add features and improve compatibility, and should be installed especially when a device misbehaves after an operating system update. Troubleshoot: if a device stops working, first check the physical connection and power; then check the device manager for warning symbols, which indicate a driver problem; try updating the driver, rolling back to a previous version if a new driver caused the fault, or uninstalling and reinstalling the driver completely. If the device still fails after a correct driver is installed, the fault is likely hardware, and the device may need repair or replacement.

Functions of common application software

Word processing software (for example Microsoft Word) creates and edits text documents: typing, formatting, spell-checking, inserting images and tables, and printing letters, reports and assignments. Spreadsheet software organizes and analyzes data in cells: entering values, calculating with formulas and functions, sorting and filtering, and showing data as charts for budgets, marks and stock records. Presentation software creates slide shows: combining text, images, charts and effects so a speaker can present ideas clearly to an audience, for lessons, business pitches and conferences. Graphic design software creates and edits visual content: drawing logos, posters and illustrations, editing photographs, and preparing layouts for print and screens, used by designers, advertisers and teachers. Together these four kinds cover the everyday work of a computer user: writing, calculating, presenting and designing.

mcqs.q: In the maintenance routine, what is removed during Step 1 (clean up the disk)?
options: Malware found by a full scan
File-system errors and bad sectors
Start-up programs and unused applications

lessons.title: Data Communication and Network Devices
lessons.notes_html:
Data communication and its components

Data communication is the exchange of data between devices through a transmission medium, following agreed rules. Its key components are the sender (the device that sends the message), the receiver (the device that receives it), the message (the data itself), the transmission medium (the path, such as a cable or wireless link, over which the data travels), and the protocol (the set of rules governing the exchange). Without all five, reliable communication cannot take place.

Routers

A router is a device that connects multiple networks and directs data packets between them. When data arrives, the router reads the destination address and chooses the best path across networks to forward it, so a message from a home network can reach a computer on the Internet. Routers therefore make communication between different networks possible, unlike switches, which only connect devices within one network.

The Network Layer of the OSI model

The Network Layer is responsible for delivering data across networks: it provides logical addressing (IP addresses) so devices on different networks can be identified, and it performs routing, choosing the path data packets take from source to destination. It sits between the Data Link Layer (node-to-node transfer on one link) and the Transport Layer (end-to-end delivery), and it is the layer where routers operate.

mcqs.q: What is data communication?
options: Storing data on a hard disk permanently
Creating documents with application software
The exchange of data between devices through a transmission medium, following agreed rules
Removing errors from a spreadsheet
mcqs.why: Data communication is the exchange of data between devices through a transmission medium, following agreed rules called protocols.

mcqs.q: In data communication, what is the sender?
options: The set of rules governing the exchange
The device that sends the message
The path over which data travels

options: The set of rules governing the exchange
The device that receives the message
The cable or wireless link used

mcqs.q: What is the transmission medium in data communication?
options: The device that sends the data
The set of rules for the exchange
The data itself

It reads the destination address and chooses the best path across networks to forward it

mcqs.why: The router reads the destination address and chooses the best path across networks to forward the data toward its destination.

options: A switch directs packets between different networks

options: Logical addressing (IP addresses)

mcqs.why: The Network Layer provides logical addressing (IP addresses) so devices on different networks can be identified, and it performs routing.

Translating a website name into a number

mcqs.why: Routing is choosing the path data packets take from source to destination, a responsibility of the Network Layer of the OSI model.

mcqs.why: The Network Layer sits between the Data Link Layer (node-to-node transfer on one link) and the Transport Layer (end-to-end delivery).

The Network Layer

mcqs.why: The Network Layer is the layer where routers operate, since routers deliver data across networks using logical addressing and routing.

lessons.title: Switching, Addresses and Protocols
lessons.notes_html:
Packet switching and circuit switching

In circuit switching, a dedicated communication path is set up between sender and receiver for the whole conversation and held until it ends, like a traditional telephone call: the path is reserved even during silences, which is reliable but wasteful. In packet switching, the message is broken into small packets that travel independently, possibly by different routes, and are reassembled at the destination, like Internet traffic: the network is used efficiently and can route around faults, but packets may arrive out of order or with delays.

DHCP: automatic IP addresses

DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses and related network settings (such as subnet mask and gateway) to devices when they join a network. Its purpose is to remove manual configuration: without DHCP, every device's address would have to be set by hand, which is slow and error-prone, and two devices could accidentally receive the same address. With DHCP, a device simply requests an address and receives a valid, unique one automatically.

Encapsulation

Encapsulation wraps data with protocol information at each layer as it travels down the sender's network stack: each layer adds its own header (and sometimes trailer) containing addressing and control information, so the data becomes a packet that only the matching layer at the receiver can unwrap. This layered wrapping organizes the data, ensures it is delivered to the correct destination in the correct form, and supports secure communication because control information and checks travel with the data and the original message is protected inside the packet structure during transmission.

TCP and UDP compared

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides reliable data transfer: it establishes a connection, numbers and acknowledges packets, retransmits lost ones, and delivers data in order and without errors, which suits file transfers, emails and web pages. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides fast but unreliable transfer: it sends packets without a connection, acknowledgements or retransmission, so packets may be lost or arrive out of order, which is acceptable for live video, voice calls and online games where speed matters more than perfect delivery.

mcqs.q: In circuit switching, what happens to the communication path during silences in a conversation?
options: It is given to another user
It stays reserved for the whole conversation, which is reliable but wasteful
It is broken into small packets
It is reassigned by DHCP
mcqs.why: In circuit switching the dedicated path is reserved even during silences, like a traditional telephone call, which is reliable but wasteful.

mcqs.q: In packet switching, how is a message sent?
options: It is broken into small packets that travel independently and are reassembled at the destination
It travels whole along one dedicated path
It is converted into a coded form first

mcqs.why: In packet switching, the message is broken into small packets that travel independently, possibly by different routes, and are reassembled at the destination.

mcqs.q: What is a possible drawback of packet switching mentioned in the notes?

mcqs.why: Packet switching uses the network efficiently and can route around faults, but packets may arrive out of order or with delays.

mcqs.q: What does DHCP automatically assign to a device joining a network?

A firewall rule and a password

mcqs.why: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses and related network settings (such as subnet mask and gateway) to devices when they join a network.

mcqs.q: What problem does DHCP help to avoid?
options: Two devices accidentally receiving the same address, and slow, error-prone manual configuration

mcqs.why: Without DHCP every address would be set by hand, which is slow and error-prone, and two devices could accidentally receive the same address.

mcqs.q: During encapsulation, what does each layer add to the data?
options: A new IP address for the device
Its own header (and sometimes trailer) containing addressing and control information
A firewall security rule

mcqs.why: Each layer adds its own header (and sometimes trailer) containing addressing and control information, so the data becomes a packet the matching layer at the receiver can unwrap.

mcqs.q: How does TCP handle packets that are lost during transfer?
options: It ignores them and continues
It asks DHCP for a new address
It converts them into coded form
It retransmits them, because it numbers and acknowledges packets
mcqs.why: TCP establishes a connection, numbers and acknowledges packets, and retransmits lost ones, delivering data in order and without errors.

mcqs.q: TCP is well suited to which kinds of traffic?
options: Live video and voice calls
File transfers, emails and web pages
Online games where speed matters most

mcqs.why: TCP's reliable, ordered, error-free delivery suits file transfers, emails and web pages, as stated in the comparison with UDP.

mcqs.q: How does UDP send packets?
options: Only after establishing a connection and receiving acknowledgements
Without a connection, acknowledgements or retransmission

mcqs.why: UDP sends packets without a connection, acknowledgements or retransmission, so packets may be lost or arrive out of order.

mcqs.q: For which uses is UDP acceptable, according to the notes?
options: Live video, voice calls and online games, where speed matters more than perfect delivery
File transfers that must be error-free

mcqs.why: UDP is acceptable for live video, voice calls and online games where speed matters more than perfect delivery of every packet.

lessons.title: Network Security and Topologies
lessons.notes_html:
Encryption in network security

Encryption converts readable data into a coded form that only the intended recipient, holding the correct key, can decode. It is important because data travelling over a network can be intercepted: without encryption, anyone capturing the traffic could read passwords, messages and financial details, but with encryption the intercepted data is meaningless to the attacker. Encryption therefore protects confidentiality and is a core method of network security alongside firewalls and antivirus software.

Advantages of the star topology

In a star topology all devices connect to a central hub or switch. Its advantages are easy fault detection and isolation: if one cable or device fails, only that device is affected and the rest of the network keeps working, and the faulty link is easy to find. It is also easy to add or remove devices without disrupting the network, and each device gets its own connection to the hub, so performance is consistent. Its main disadvantage is dependence on the central hub: if the hub fails, the whole network fails.

Firewalls

A firewall monitors and controls network traffic passing between a trusted internal network and untrusted outside networks, such as the Internet. It applies security rules to incoming and outgoing packets, blocking unauthorized access attempts and suspicious traffic while allowing legitimate communication through. By acting as a barrier at the network boundary, it prevents attackers from reaching internal devices and stops malicious data from entering or leaving the network.

mcqs.q: What does encryption do to data?
options: Converts readable data into a coded form that only the intended recipient, holding the correct key, can decode
Breaks data into packets for transmission
Assigns addresses to devices on a network

mcqs.why: Encryption converts readable data into a coded form that only the intended recipient, holding the correct key, can decode.

mcqs.q: If encrypted traffic is intercepted by an attacker, what does the attacker get?
options: The user's passwords in readable form
The financial details in plain text
The original messages unchanged
Data that is meaningless to the attacker
mcqs.why: Without encryption, anyone capturing traffic could read passwords, messages and financial details, but with encryption the intercepted data is meaningless to the attacker.

mcqs.q: What does encryption protect in network security?
options: Confidentiality of the data
The speed of the network
The addressing of packets
The cabling of the network
mcqs.why: Encryption protects confidentiality and is a core method of network security alongside firewalls and antivirus software.

mcqs.q: In a star topology, what happens if one cable or device fails?
options: The whole network stops working
All data takes a longer ring path
Only that device is affected and the rest of the network keeps working

mcqs.why: In a star topology, if one cable or device fails, only that device is affected and the rest of the network keeps working, and the faulty link is easy to find.

mcqs.q: What is the main disadvantage of a star topology?
options: Faults are hard to isolate
Devices cannot be added easily

mcqs.why: The main disadvantage of the star topology is dependence on the central hub: if the hub fails, the whole network fails.

mcqs.q: Why is a star topology easy to manage when the network changes?
options: Devices can be added or removed without disrupting the network
It needs no central hub at all

mcqs.why: A star topology is easy to add or remove devices without disrupting the network, and each device gets its own connection to the hub.

mcqs.q: Between which networks does a firewall monitor and control traffic?
options: Between two devices on the same hub
Between a sender and a receiver on one link
Between a trusted internal network and untrusted outside networks, such as the Internet
Between two printers in an office
mcqs.why: A firewall monitors and controls network traffic passing between a trusted internal network and untrusted outside networks, such as the Internet.

mcqs.q: How does a firewall treat different kinds of traffic?
options: It blocks all incoming and outgoing packets
It blocks unauthorized access attempts and suspicious traffic while allowing legitimate communication through
It allows all traffic but records it
It translates all traffic into IP addresses
mcqs.why: A firewall applies security rules to incoming and outgoing packets, blocking unauthorized access attempts and suspicious traffic while allowing legitimate communication through.

mcqs.q: How does a firewall protect internal devices?
options: By acting as a barrier at the network boundary, preventing attackers from reaching internal devices
By converting their data into a coded form
By assigning each device a unique address
By connecting them all to a central hub
mcqs.why: By acting as a barrier at the network boundary, a firewall prevents attackers from reaching internal devices and stops malicious data from entering or leaving.

mcqs.q: Alongside firewalls and antivirus software, encryption is described as what?
options: A method of assigning IP addresses
A topology for connecting devices

mcqs.why: Encryption protects confidentiality and is a core method of network security alongside firewalls and antivirus software.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes: Objectives, Switching and Protocols
lessons.notes_html:
Objectives of computer networks

A computer network is a system of linked devices and computers that work together to facilitate communication. Its objectives are resource sharing, communication and data management. Resource sharing means multiple users share expensive resources instead of each needing their own: for example, several office computers share one printer and one Internet connection, and employees share files stored on a central server. Data communication means fast exchange of information between devices and users: for example, sending an email from one office to another, or students in different classrooms accessing the same learning material online. Together these objectives make work cheaper and faster: a business avoids buying a printer for every desk, a school gives every student access to the same digital library, and a hospital lets doctors in different departments view the same patient records.

Transmission time: a worked calculation

Time = amount of data divided by transmission rate. (a) 10 kilobits = 10,000 bits. Time = 10,000 / 500 = 20 seconds. (b) 10 kilobytes must first be converted to bits: 1 byte = 8 bits, so 10 kilobytes = 10 x 8 = 80 kilobits = 80,000 bits. Time = 80,000 / 500 = 160 seconds (2 minutes 40 seconds). The kilobyte message therefore takes eight times longer than the kilobit message, because a byte holds eight bits.

Data transmission: packet and circuit switching

In circuit switching, before any data flows, a dedicated communication path is established between sender and receiver and reserved for the entire session, then released when the session ends. This guarantees a constant path and steady delivery, which suits voice calls, but it wastes capacity during pauses, since no one else can use the reserved path. In packet switching, the message is divided into small packets, each labelled with source and destination addresses; packets travel independently across the network, possibly taking different routes according to current traffic, and are reassembled in order at the destination. This uses the network efficiently, lets traffic route around failed links, and suits bursty data such as web browsing, but it needs extra work to reassemble packets and handle any that are lost or delayed. Modern computer networks, including the Internet, use packet switching.

Protocols: TCP/IP, HTTP, DNS and DHCP

Protocols are the agreed rules that govern data communication: without them, devices from different makers could not understand each other. They define message formats, addressing, error handling and the order of exchange, so communication is reliable and predictable. Key protocols: TCP/IP is the core protocol suite of the Internet — IP addresses packets and routes them across networks, while TCP provides reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of the data. HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) governs how web browsers request and receive web pages from servers. DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (such as a website name) into IP addresses computers use, so users need not remember numbers. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically assigns IP addresses and network settings to devices joining a network, avoiding manual configuration and address clashes. Together these protocols let a user type a website name and reliably receive the correct page.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of resource sharing in a network?
options: A student submitting work online

mcqs.why: Resource sharing means multiple users share expensive resources: several office computers share one printer and one Internet connection, and employees share files on a central server.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of data communication as a network objective?
options: Sending an email from one office to another

mcqs.why: Data communication means fast exchange of information between devices and users, for example sending an email from one office to another.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for transmission time given in the notes?
options: Time = transmission rate divided by amount of data
Time = amount of data divided by transmission rate
Time = amount of data multiplied by transmission rate
Time = transmission rate minus amount of data
mcqs.why: The notes give the worked formula: Time = amount of data divided by transmission rate, used in both calculations that follow.

mcqs.q: How long does it take to send 10 kilobits at a transmission rate of 500 bits per second? (10 kilobits = 10,000 bits)
options: 5 seconds
50 seconds
2 seconds
20 seconds
mcqs.why: Working: 10 kilobits = 10,000 bits. Time = amount of data / transmission rate = 10,000 / 500 = 20 seconds, exactly as in the notes' worked calculation.

mcqs.q: How long does it take to send 10 kilobytes at a transmission rate of 500 bits per second? (1 byte = 8 bits)
options: 20 seconds
80 seconds
160 seconds (2 minutes 40 seconds)
1,600 seconds
mcqs.why: Working: 10 kilobytes = 10 x 8 = 80 kilobits = 80,000 bits. Time = 80,000 / 500 = 160 seconds, which is 2 minutes 40 seconds, as worked in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why does the 10-kilobyte message take eight times longer than the 10-kilobit message at the same rate?
options: Because kilobytes travel by a different route
Because a byte holds eight bits
Because the rate changes for larger messages
Because packets are reassembled at the destination
mcqs.why: The kilobyte message takes eight times longer (160 s vs 20 s) because a byte holds eight bits, so 10 kilobytes contain eight times as many bits.

mcqs.q: In circuit switching, when is the dedicated path released?
options: When the session ends, after being reserved for the entire session
After each packet is sent
Whenever there is a silence in the call
When a fault occurs on another link
mcqs.why: In circuit switching a dedicated path is established before data flows, reserved for the entire session, then released when the session ends.

mcqs.q: Which switching method do modern computer networks, including the Internet, use?
options: Circuit switching
Message switching by dedicated path

mcqs.why: The notes state that modern computer networks, including the Internet, use packet switching, where packets travel independently and are reassembled at the destination.

mcqs.q: In the TCP/IP suite, what is the role of IP?
options: It requests web pages from servers
It addresses packets and routes them across networks
It translates domain names into addresses
It assigns addresses automatically to new devices
mcqs.why: In TCP/IP, IP addresses packets and routes them across networks, while TCP provides reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of the data.

mcqs.q: What does HTTP govern?
options: How IP addresses are assigned to devices
How domain names are translated
How web browsers request and receive web pages from servers
How packets are reassembled at the destination
mcqs.why: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) governs how web browsers request and receive web pages from servers, as described in the protocols section.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes: Security, Applications and Topologies
lessons.notes_html:
Network security methods evaluated

Firewalls monitor and control network traffic at the boundary between a trusted network and the outside world, blocking unauthorized access while allowing legitimate traffic; their strength is perimeter protection, but they cannot stop threats already inside the network or a user deliberately downloading malware. Encryption converts data into a code readable only with the correct key, protecting confidentiality even if traffic is intercepted; its strength is that stolen data stays useless, but it depends on keys being kept secret and adds processing overhead. Antivirus software detects, quarantines and removes malware on individual devices, protecting against viruses that arrive by email, download or USB drive; its strength is device-level defence, but it must be kept updated to recognize new threats. No single method is enough: effective security combines all three — firewall at the boundary, encryption on the data, and antivirus on the devices — plus strong passwords and regular updates.

Networks in business, education and healthcare

In business, networks enable resource sharing and efficient communication: employees share printers, files and a single Internet connection, branches communicate by email and video conferencing, and online sales and banking run over networks. In education, networks give students and teachers access to shared learning resources: a school network lets every classroom reach the same digital library and learning platform, students submit work online, and classes can join video lessons with experts elsewhere. In healthcare, networks let hospitals share patient records between departments, doctors consult specialists remotely, and medical devices send monitoring data to central systems, so treatment is faster and better coordinated. In each field the same network benefits appear: shared resources, faster communication and access to information from many locations.

Network topologies compared

In a star topology all devices connect to a central hub or switch: a single device failure affects only that device and faults are easy to find, but the hub is a single point of failure and cabling costs are higher. In a ring topology each device connects to two neighbours forming a closed loop, and data travels around the ring: it is simple and orderly, but one broken link or device can disrupt the whole ring. In a bus topology all devices share one central cable (the backbone): it is cheap and easy to install for small networks, but a break in the backbone disables the whole network and faults are hard to isolate. In a mesh topology every device connects to many or all others: it is the most reliable, since data can take alternative routes if a link fails, but it is the most expensive and complex to cable and manage. Choice depends on need: star for most offices, bus for small cheap setups, ring where order matters, and mesh where reliability is critical.

mcqs.q: What is a limitation of a firewall, according to the evaluation in the notes?
options: It cannot allow legitimate traffic through
It cannot stop threats already inside the network or a user deliberately downloading malware
It cannot monitor traffic at the boundary
It cannot block unauthorized access
mcqs.why: A firewall's strength is perimeter protection, but it cannot stop threats already inside the network or a user deliberately downloading malware.

mcqs.q: What does the strength of encryption depend on, and what does it cost?
options: It depends on the speed of the network and costs extra cabling
It depends on the firewall rules and costs a new hub
It depends on keys being kept secret and adds processing overhead
It depends on antivirus updates and costs disk space
mcqs.why: Encryption's strength is that stolen data stays useless, but it depends on keys being kept secret and adds processing overhead.

So it can monitor traffic at the boundary
So it can encrypt data on the devices
To recognize new threats, since it protects individual devices against viruses
mcqs.why: Antivirus software gives device-level defence against viruses arriving by email, download or USB drive, but it must be kept updated to recognize new threats.

mcqs.q: What does effective network security combine?
options: Firewall at the boundary, encryption on the data, and antivirus on the devices, plus strong passwords and regular updates
Only a firewall at the boundary
Only encryption on the data
Only antivirus on the devices
mcqs.why: No single method is enough: effective security combines all three, firewall at the boundary, encryption on the data, and antivirus on the devices, plus strong passwords and regular updates.

mcqs.q: How do networks help business branches communicate?

By printing records in each branch
By storing backups on USB drives
By connecting devices in a closed ring

mcqs.q: How do networks help in education, according to the notes?

Doctors consult specialists remotely
Employees share one printer per office
A school network lets every classroom reach the same digital library and learning platform
mcqs.why: In education, a school network lets every classroom reach the same digital library and learning platform, students submit work online, and classes join video lessons with experts elsewhere.

mcqs.q: How do networks help in healthcare?
options: Hospitals share patient records between departments and doctors consult specialists remotely
Students submit work online to teachers
Branches run online sales and banking
Devices connect to a central hub in a star

mcqs.q: What is a weakness of a ring topology?

It is the most expensive topology to cable
One broken link or device can disrupt the whole ring
The central hub is a single point of failure
mcqs.why: In a ring topology each device connects to two neighbours forming a closed loop; it is simple and orderly, but one broken link or device can disrupt the whole ring.

mcqs.q: What happens in a bus topology if the backbone cable breaks?

The whole network is disabled

The hub takes over the connections

mcqs.q: Why is a mesh topology the most reliable, and what is its drawback?

It forms a closed loop, but one break disrupts it
mcqs.why: In a mesh topology every device connects to many or all others, so data can take alternative routes if a link fails, making it most reliable but most expensive and complex.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes: Worked Calculations
lessons.notes_html:
Shift cipher: a worked example

(a) Encrypt by shifting each letter 4 places forward in the alphabet: S->W, E->I, C->G, U->Y, R->V, I->M, T->X, Y->C. The encrypted message is WIGYVMXC. (b) Decrypt by shifting each letter 4 places back: W->S, M->I, X->T, Y->U, V->R, M->I, I->E. The decrypted result is SITURIE. Note: SITURIE is not an English word, and the book's ciphertext WMXYVMI does not decrypt to a recognizable word under a shift of 4; the ciphertext as printed appears to contain a misprint, since encrypting SECURITY with a shift of 4 gives WIGYVMXC, not WMXYVMI. The mechanical decryption above follows the book's stated shift exactly.

IPv4 addresses: a worked calculation

(a) Each of the 32 bits can be 0 or 1, so the total number of unique addresses is 2 to the power 32. 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 — approximately 4.3 billion addresses. (b) 10% reserved for special purposes = 10% of 4,294,967,296 = 429,496,729.6, about 429,496,730 addresses. Addresses left = 4,294,967,296 - 429,496,730 = 3,865,470,566, about 3.87 billion addresses (90% of the total). This calculation shows why the 32-bit IPv4 space, once thought ample, is now exhausted in practice, which is why the much larger IPv6 space was introduced.

options: W
O
T
X
mcqs.why: Working: shifting each letter 4 places forward in the alphabet, S -> W (S, T, U, V, W). The notes' worked example begins S->W when encrypting SECURITY.

mcqs.q: In a shift cipher with a shift of 4 places forward, the letter E becomes which letter?
options: A
F
I
C
mcqs.why: Working: shifting 4 places forward, E -> I (E, F, G, H, I). The notes' worked example lists E->I when encrypting SECURITY with a shift of 4.

mcqs.q: Encrypt the word SECURITY using a shift cipher with a shift of 4 places forward.
options: WMXYVMI
WIGYVMXC
WIGYVNXC
SECURITY
mcqs.why: Working, shifting each letter 4 forward: S->W, E->I, C->G, U->Y, R->V, I->M, T->X, Y->C, giving WIGYVMXC, exactly as worked in the notes.

mcqs.q: Decrypt the letter W by shifting 4 places back in a shift cipher.
options: A
T
U
S
mcqs.why: Working: shifting 4 places back, W -> S (W, V, U, T, S). The notes' decryption example begins W->S when shifting each letter 4 places back.

mcqs.q: Following the book's stated shift of 4 places back, decrypting the ciphertext WMXYVMI gives what result?
options: SITURIE
SECURIT
WIGYVMX
RESTORE
mcqs.why: Working, shifting each letter 4 back: W->S, M->I, X->T, Y->U, V->R, M->I, I->E, giving SITURIE, the mechanical decryption result given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why do the notes say the book's ciphertext WMXYVMI appears to contain a misprint?
options: Because it has too few letters to be a word
Because it cannot be shifted by 4 at all
Because encrypting SECURITY with a shift of 4 gives WIGYVMXC, not WMXYVMI
Because SITURIE is a real English word
mcqs.why: Encrypting SECURITY with a shift of 4 gives WIGYVMXC, not WMXYVMI, and SITURIE is not an English word, so the ciphertext as printed appears to contain a misprint.

mcqs.q: An IPv4 address has 32 bits, and each bit can be 0 or 1. How many unique IPv4 addresses are there in total?
mcqs.why: Working: each of the 32 bits can be 0 or 1, so the total is 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 unique addresses, approximately 4.3 billion, as calculated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Approximately how large is the total IPv4 address space?
options: About 429 million addresses
About 4.3 billion addresses
About 3.87 million addresses
About 43 billion addresses
mcqs.why: Working: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296, which is approximately 4.3 billion addresses, the approximation used in the notes' IPv4 calculation.

mcqs.q: If 10% of all IPv4 addresses are reserved for special purposes, about how many addresses is that?
options: About 42,949,673 addresses
About 3,865,470,566 addresses
About 429,496,730 addresses
About 4,294,967,296 addresses
mcqs.why: Working: 10% of 4,294,967,296 = 429,496,729.6, which is about 429,496,730 addresses reserved for special purposes, as calculated in the notes.

mcqs.q: After reserving 10% for special purposes, how many IPv4 addresses are left?
options: 3,865,470,566 addresses (about 3.87 billion)
4,294,967,296 addresses
429,496,730 addresses
3,294,967,296 addresses
mcqs.why: Working: addresses left = 4,294,967,296 - 429,496,730 = 3,865,470,566, about 3.87 billion addresses (90% of the total), as calculated in the notes.

lessons.title: The Four Pillars of Computational Thinking
lessons.notes_html:
Computational thinking

Computational thinking is a problem-solving approach that employs systematic, algorithmic and logical thinking. It means tackling a problem the way a computer scientist would: understanding it clearly, breaking it into parts, spotting patterns, ignoring irrelevant detail, and designing a clear step-by-step solution that could be carried out by a person or a computer.

Decomposition

Decomposition is breaking a large, complex problem into smaller, more manageable parts, each of which can be understood and solved separately. For example, organizing a school event decomposes into booking a venue, arranging transport, preparing food, and inviting guests. It simplifies problems because each small part is easier to solve than the whole, and the solutions combine into the full answer.

Pattern recognition

Pattern recognition is finding and using similarities within problems: when you notice that a new problem resembles one you have solved before, you can reuse the earlier solution pattern. For example, once you learn the pattern for finding the largest of three numbers (compare the first two, keep the larger, compare it with the third), you can apply the same pattern to find the largest score in a class list, or the oldest student in a group — the data changes, but the pattern stays the same.

Abstraction

Abstraction is ignoring the details to focus on the main idea: keeping only the information relevant to the problem and hiding the rest. It is important because real problems carry far more detail than a solution needs — for example, a map for navigation shows roads and landmarks but hides trees, house colours and shop interiors, and a driver can still reach the destination. By abstracting, you simplify the problem and avoid being distracted by irrelevant detail.

Algorithms

An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem, written clearly enough that it can be followed exactly and always gives the same result for the same input. Examples are a recipe for cooking, directions for reaching a place, and the steps for adding two numbers. An algorithm must be unambiguous, finite (it must end), and effective (each step must be doable).

mcqs.why: The notes say computational thinking means tackling a problem the way a computer scientist would: understanding it clearly, breaking it into parts, spotting patterns and designing a clear step-by-step solution.

mcqs.why: The notes decompose organising a school event into booking a venue, arranging transport, preparing food and inviting guests; booking a venue is one of those parts.

mcqs.why: Abstraction is important because real problems carry far more detail than a solution needs; keeping only relevant information simplifies the problem and avoids distraction.

lessons.title: Representing Algorithms
lessons.notes_html:
Understanding the problem

Problem understanding is the first step of problem-solving, and it helps because you cannot design a correct solution for a problem you have not understood: you must know what is given (the inputs), what is required (the output), and what constraints apply. For example, before writing a grading algorithm you must know the exact mark ranges for each grade; without that, even a perfect algorithm would give wrong grades. Understanding the problem also prevents wasted work on the wrong solution.

Flowcharts

A flowchart is a graphical representation of an algorithm, using standard shapes connected by arrows: ovals for start and end, parallelograms for input and output, rectangles for processing steps, and diamonds for decisions. Flowcharts are used to design, visualize and communicate an algorithm before coding, because the flow of steps and decisions can be seen at a glance, errors are easier to spot, and the design can be discussed with others who may not read code.

Pseudocode

Pseudocode is a high-level description of an algorithm using plain language, written in a structured, code-like style but without the strict syntax of a programming language. Its purpose is to plan an algorithm in a form that is easy to read, check and translate into any programming language later. It bridges the gap between a human idea and actual code: you work out the logic first, then implement it in Python, Java or another language.

Flowcharts and pseudocode compared

Both describe algorithms, but flowcharts represent them graphically with shapes and arrows, while pseudocode describes them in written, plain-language steps. Flowcharts are better for seeing the overall flow and decision branches at a glance, and for explaining an algorithm to others visually; pseudocode is better for detailed, step-heavy logic and converts more directly into code. In practice they complement each other: a flowchart shows the structure, pseudocode spells out the details.

lessons.title: Testing Algorithms: Dry Runs and Debugging
lessons.notes_html:
Dry runs

A dry run is manually going through an algorithm or flowchart with sample data, step by step, tracking how values change, to identify any errors before the program is written or run. It is important because it catches logic errors early — wrong conditions, missed cases, incorrect calculations — when they are still cheap and easy to fix, and it confirms that the algorithm actually produces the expected output for known inputs.

LARP: learning algorithms by acting them out

LARP stands for Logic of Algorithm for Resolution of Problems. It is a fun, interactive way to learn how algorithms work by actually running them and seeing the results — learners act out or simulate the steps of an algorithm, for example by physically sorting cards to follow a sorting algorithm, instead of only reading about it. Its significance is that it makes abstract algorithmic thinking concrete and memorable: by experiencing each step, learners understand why the algorithm works and where it can go wrong.

Debugging techniques

Two debugging techniques are dry running and simulation. Dry running means manually tracing the algorithm with sample data, recording each variable's value at each step, to find where the actual behaviour diverges from the expected behaviour. Simulation means using a computer program or model to imitate the real process — for example, running a flowchart in a simulator or testing code with test data — so errors can be observed safely without affecting a real system. Both techniques find and help fix errors (bugs) in an algorithm or flowchart; a third approach is testing with boundary values, such as the smallest and largest allowed inputs.

mcqs.why: A dry run is manually going through an algorithm or flowchart with sample data, step by step, tracking how values change, to identify errors before the program is written or run.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes: Computational Thinking and Its Pillars
lessons.notes_html:
Computational thinking and its significance

Computational thinking is a problem-solving approach that employs systematic, algorithmic and logical thinking, built on four pillars: decomposition (breaking problems into parts), pattern recognition (finding similarities), abstraction (focusing on relevant detail only) and algorithm design (creating step-by-step solutions). Its significance is that it gives a reliable method for tackling complex problems in any field, not just computing: it turns vague, overwhelming problems into clear, solvable steps. In business, a shopkeeper decomposes monthly sales analysis into collecting daily sales, grouping by product, finding patterns (which products sell best on weekends) and designing a reordering routine. In medicine, doctors use pattern recognition (symptoms matching known conditions) and abstraction (ignoring irrelevant patient details) to diagnose. In science, researchers design algorithms to process experimental data. In everyday life, planning a journey uses decomposition (route, transport, timing), abstraction (ignoring irrelevant streets) and an algorithm (the sequence of turns). Computational thinking is therefore a general life skill for the modern world, where data and systems surround every decision.

Decomposition in detail

Decomposition is the process of breaking a large, complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems that can each be solved separately and then combined. It is important for three reasons. First, it simplifies: a small part is easier to understand, solve and test than the whole — for example, building a school website decomposes into designing pages, writing content, adding images and testing links, and each task can be given to a different person. Second, it enables reuse: a sub-problem solved once (such as a login routine) can be reused wherever it appears. Third, it makes errors easier to find: when a part fails, you know which part to fix, rather than searching the whole problem. Without decomposition, complex problems remain overwhelming and error-prone; with it, even very large systems become a collection of solvable pieces.

Pattern recognition in detail

Pattern recognition is finding and using similarities within problems — noticing that parts of a new problem match parts of problems already solved, or that data contains repeating trends. It helps in three ways. First, it enables reuse: if you recognize that computing a class average follows the same pattern as computing a shop's daily average (sum the values, divide by the count), you do not need to invent a new method. Second, it reveals predictions: spotting that sales rise every weekend lets a shopkeeper stock accordingly. Third, it simplifies algorithms: a sorting pattern learned once (compare neighbours, swap if out of order) applies to numbers, names and dates alike. In short, patterns turn new problems into familiar ones, so solutions become faster, more reliable and easier to generalize.

Abstraction in detail

Abstraction is the process of ignoring details to focus on the main idea — keeping only the information relevant to the problem and hiding the rest. Its importance is that real problems carry overwhelming detail, and abstraction lets you reason about the essentials: without it, every problem would be too complex to model or solve. Examples: a road map abstracts a city to roads and landmarks, hiding trees and building colours, yet it is exactly what a driver needs; a weather app abstracts atmospheric physics into a simple forecast (sunny, 28 degrees), hiding the equations behind it; in programming, a 'print' command abstracts away the printer's hardware details, letting the programmer focus on what to print. In each case abstraction simplifies the problem to a manageable model while preserving what matters for the solution.

mcqs.q: Computational thinking is built on four pillars. Which set lists them correctly?
options: Decomposition, guessing, abstraction, coding
Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithm design
Pattern recognition, memorisation, drawing, testing
Abstraction, coding, simulation, printing
mcqs.why: The four pillars are decomposition (breaking problems into parts), pattern recognition (finding similarities), abstraction (focusing on relevant detail only) and algorithm design (creating step-by-step solutions).

mcqs.q: What is the significance of computational thinking, according to the detailed notes?
options: It is useful only for computer programmers
It replaces the need to solve problems step by step
It turns vague, overwhelming problems into clear, solvable steps
It works only for problems involving numbers
mcqs.why: Its significance is that it gives a reliable method for tackling complex problems in any field, turning vague, overwhelming problems into clear, solvable steps.

mcqs.q: Decomposition enables reuse. Which example of reuse is given in the notes?
options: A login routine solved once can be reused wherever it appears
A road map can be used as a weather forecast
A recipe can be used to grade students
A sorting pattern can print documents
mcqs.why: The notes say a sub-problem solved once, such as a login routine, can be reused wherever it appears, instead of being solved again from scratch.

mcqs.q: How does decomposition make errors easier to find?
options: It hides which part of the problem failed
It removes all errors automatically
It combines every part into one large step
When a part fails, you know which part to fix instead of searching the whole problem
mcqs.why: With decomposition, when a part fails you know which part to fix, rather than searching the whole problem; without it, complex problems remain overwhelming and error-prone.

mcqs.q: Which example shows pattern recognition being used to make a prediction?
options: A driver follows a road map to a destination
Sales rise every weekend, so a shopkeeper stocks accordingly
A programmer uses a print command
A class builds a school website in parts
mcqs.why: Spotting that sales rise every weekend lets a shopkeeper stock accordingly: the recognised pattern in the data reveals a prediction about future sales.

mcqs.q: Computing a class average follows the same pattern as computing a shop's daily average. What is that pattern?
options: Sum the values, then divide by the count
Compare neighbours and swap if out of order
Keep the largest value and discard the rest
Ignore the details and draw a map
mcqs.why: Both averages follow the same pattern stated in the notes: sum the values, divide by the count, so no new method needs to be invented.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of abstraction in programming given in the notes?
options: Sorting numbers by comparing neighbours
Dividing a website into pages and content
A 'print' command abstracts away the printer's hardware details
Matching symptoms to known conditions
mcqs.why: In programming, a 'print' command abstracts away the printer's hardware details, letting the programmer focus on what to print rather than how the printer works.

mcqs.q: How does a weather app use abstraction, according to the notes?
options: It shows every atmospheric equation to the user
It breaks the weather into daily parts
It compares today's weather with yesterday's
It abstracts atmospheric physics into a simple forecast such as sunny, 28 degrees
mcqs.why: A weather app abstracts atmospheric physics into a simple forecast (sunny, 28 degrees), hiding the equations behind it while preserving what matters for the user.

mcqs.q: In medicine, how do doctors use pattern recognition, according to the notes?
options: By matching symptoms to known conditions
By ignoring all patient details
By designing routines for reordering stock
By processing experimental data with algorithms
mcqs.why: The notes say doctors use pattern recognition (symptoms matching known conditions) and abstraction (ignoring irrelevant patient details) to diagnose illness.

mcqs.q: Planning a journey uses an algorithm. In that example, what is the algorithm?
options: The choice of transport
The sequence of turns
The list of irrelevant streets
The timing of the trip
mcqs.why: In the journey example, decomposition covers route, transport and timing, abstraction ignores irrelevant streets, and the algorithm is the sequence of turns followed to reach the destination.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes: Designing Algorithms
lessons.notes_html:
Worked algorithm: assigning grades from marks

Step 1: Start. Step 2: Input the student's marks. Step 3: If marks are 90 or above, assign grade A+. Step 4: Else, if marks are between 80 and 89, assign grade A. Step 5: Else, if marks are between 70 and 79, assign grade B. Step 6: Else, if marks are between 60 and 69, assign grade C. Step 7: Else (marks below 60), assign grade F. Step 8: Output the grade. Step 9: Stop. Dry run check: marks 85 reach Step 4 (80 to 89) and give A; marks 59 fall through all conditions to Step 7 and give F; marks 90 give A+ at Step 3.

Designing a solution with flowcharts and pseudocode: the library example

To solve a complex problem, first understand it and decompose it into smaller parts, then design the solution with flowcharts and pseudocode before coding. Example: a library wants to find overdue books. Decomposition: (a) read each book's due date and today's date, (b) compare them, (c) list books past their due date, (d) print borrower details. Flowchart: start (oval) -> input today's date and book records (parallelogram) -> for each book, is due date before today? (diamond) -> if yes, add to overdue list (rectangle); if no, skip -> more books? (diamond) -> if yes, repeat; if no, print overdue list (parallelogram) -> stop (oval). Pseudocode: Start; Input today; For each book record: If due date < today Then add book to overdue list; End For; Print overdue list; Stop. The flowchart shows the flow and decisions visually, the pseudocode spells out the exact logic, and a dry run with sample dates verifies the design before any code is written.

Algorithms and their role, with a worked example and flowchart

An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem, precise enough to be followed exactly and to finish with a correct result. Its role in computational thinking is central: decomposition, pattern recognition and abstraction prepare the problem, but the algorithm is the actual solution — the ordered procedure that a person or computer executes. Example: finding the largest of three numbers. Algorithm: Step 1: Start. Step 2: Input A, B, C. Step 3: Set Largest = A. Step 4: If B > Largest, set Largest = B. Step 5: If C > Largest, set Largest = C. Step 6: Output Largest. Step 7: Stop. Corresponding flowchart: Start (oval) -> Input A, B, C (parallelogram) -> Largest = A (rectangle) -> Is B > Largest? (diamond) -> if yes, Largest = B (rectangle), then -> Is C > Largest? (diamond) -> if yes, Largest = C (rectangle), then -> Output Largest (parallelogram) -> Stop (oval). A dry run with A=5, B=9, C=7 gives Largest=9, confirming the design.

mcqs.q: Using the grading algorithm in the notes, what grade do marks of 85 receive?
options: A+
B
F
A
mcqs.why: Trace: Step 3 checks marks >= 90 — 85 fails. Step 4 checks 80 to 89 — 85 is in this range, so grade A is assigned, exactly as the notes' dry run check states.

mcqs.q: Using the grading algorithm in the notes, what grade do marks of 59 receive?
options: C
F
B
A
mcqs.why: Trace: 59 is below 90, below 80, below 70 and below 60, so it falls through all conditions to Step 7 (marks below 60), which assigns grade F.

mcqs.q: Using the grading algorithm in the notes, what grade do marks of 90 receive?
options: A
B
A+
F
mcqs.why: Trace: Step 3 checks whether marks are 90 or above. 90 meets this condition, so grade A+ is assigned at Step 3, as the notes' dry run check confirms.

mcqs.q: Using the grading algorithm in the notes, what grade do marks of 75 receive?
options: B
A
C
A+
mcqs.why: Trace: 75 is below 90 and below 80, then Step 5 checks 70 to 79 — 75 is in this range, so grade B is assigned.

mcqs.q: In the largest-of-three-numbers algorithm, what does Step 3 do?
options: Inputs A, B and C
Outputs the largest value
Compares C with Largest
Sets Largest = A
mcqs.why: The algorithm's steps are: Start; Input A, B, C; Step 3 sets Largest = A; then B and C are each compared with Largest before the result is output.

mcqs.q: Dry run the largest-of-three algorithm with A = 5, B = 9, C = 7. What is output?
mcqs.why: Trace: Largest = A = 5. B = 9 > 5, so Largest = 9. C = 7 is not greater than 9, so Largest stays 9. Output is 9, confirming the design as the notes state.

mcqs.q: Dry run the largest-of-three algorithm with A = 2, B = 1, C = 8. What is output?
mcqs.why: Trace: Largest = A = 2. B = 1 is not greater than 2, so Largest stays 2. C = 8 > 2, so Largest = 8. Output is 8.

mcqs.q: In the library overdue-books example, decomposition part (b) is which task?
options: Compare each book's due date with today's date
Read each book's due date and today's date
List the books past their due date
Print the borrower details
mcqs.why: The decomposition is: (a) read each book's due date and today's date, (b) compare them, (c) list books past their due date, (d) print borrower details — so comparing is part (b).

mcqs.q: In the library pseudocode, what happens when a book's due date is before today?
options: The book is printed immediately
The loop stops at once
The book is added to the overdue list
The borrower details are deleted
mcqs.why: The pseudocode says: For each book record, If due date < today Then add book to overdue list; after the loop the overdue list is printed.

mcqs.q: In the library flowchart, the question 'Is due date before today?' is drawn inside which shape?
options: Oval
Parallelogram
Rectangle
Diamond
mcqs.why: Decisions in a flowchart are drawn as diamonds: 'is due date before today?' is a yes/no decision, so it sits in a diamond, with yes leading to adding the book to the overdue list.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes: Flowcharts, Pseudocode and Dry Runs
lessons.notes_html:
Flowcharts and pseudocode: advantages and disadvantages

Flowcharts represent algorithms graphically with shapes (ovals, parallelograms, rectangles, diamonds) joined by arrows; pseudocode describes them in plain-language, structured written steps. Flowchart advantages: the flow and decision branches are visible at a glance, errors in logic are easy to spot, and non-programmers can follow them — for example, explaining a school admission process to office staff. Disadvantages: large algorithms make huge, cluttered diagrams that are hard to draw, modify and print. Pseudocode advantages: it is compact, easy to edit, handles detailed logic well, and translates almost directly into code — for example, drafting a sorting routine before coding it in Python. Disadvantages: it has no strict standard, so different writers use different styles, and it cannot show overall flow as instantly as a diagram. In practice, use a flowchart when the audience needs the big picture or the algorithm is decision-heavy, and pseudocode when the logic is detailed or coding is the next step; many designers use both.

Dry runs and validation

A dry run is manually going through an algorithm with sample data, tracking every variable step by step, without running it on a computer. With a flowchart, you follow the arrows with a chosen input, writing down the value of each variable at each shape, and checking that the path taken matches expectations. With pseudocode, you read each written step in order, updating a trace table of variable values as you go. It validates correctness in three ways: it confirms the algorithm produces the expected output for known inputs; it reveals logic errors (wrong conditions, missing cases, infinite loops) before coding, when fixes are cheap; and it tests edge cases, such as the smallest, largest and boundary inputs (for example marks of 59, 60, 89 and 90 in a grading algorithm). An algorithm that passes dry runs on varied sample data is far more likely to be correct when finally coded.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an advantage of flowcharts?
options: The flow and decision branches are visible at a glance
They handle very detailed logic in very little space
They translate almost directly into code
They follow one strict written standard
mcqs.why: Flowchart advantages in the notes: the flow and decision branches are visible at a glance, errors in logic are easy to spot, and non-programmers can follow them.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a disadvantage of flowcharts?
options: They cannot show decisions at all
Non-programmers cannot follow them
Large algorithms make huge, cluttered diagrams that are hard to draw, modify and print
They are too compact to read
mcqs.why: The stated disadvantage is that large algorithms make huge, cluttered flowchart diagrams that are hard to draw, modify and print.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an advantage of pseudocode?
options: It shows overall flow more instantly than a diagram
It has a strict standard every writer follows
It can be executed directly by a computer
It translates almost directly into code
mcqs.why: Pseudocode advantages in the notes: it is compact, easy to edit, handles detailed logic well, and translates almost directly into code, for example drafting a sorting routine before coding it in Python.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a disadvantage of pseudocode?
options: It cannot handle detailed logic
It has no strict standard, so different writers use different styles
It is hard to edit once written
It produces cluttered diagrams
mcqs.why: Pseudocode's disadvantages are that it has no strict standard, so different writers use different styles, and it cannot show overall flow as instantly as a diagram.

mcqs.q: When should a flowchart be used, according to the notes?
options: When the audience needs the big picture or the algorithm is decision-heavy
When the logic is very detailed and coding is the next step
When the algorithm must be typed quickly
When no decisions are involved at all
mcqs.why: Use a flowchart when the audience needs the big picture or the algorithm is decision-heavy; use pseudocode when the logic is detailed or coding is the next step — many designers use both.

mcqs.q: In a dry run of a flowchart, what do you do?
options: Run the flowchart in a simulator program
Redraw the flowchart with new shapes
Skip the decision shapes and read only rectangles
Follow the arrows with a chosen input, writing down the value of each variable at each shape
mcqs.why: With a flowchart dry run, you follow the arrows with a chosen input, writing down the value of each variable at each shape, and check that the path taken matches expectations.

mcqs.q: Which set of marks is given in the notes as boundary inputs for testing a grading algorithm?
mcqs.why: Dry runs test edge cases such as the smallest, largest and boundary inputs — for example marks of 59, 60, 89 and 90 in a grading algorithm, which sit either side of grade boundaries.

mcqs.q: A dry run can reveal which kinds of problems before coding?
options: Slow computer hardware
Missing printer paper
Wrong conditions, missing cases and infinite loops
Incorrect file names
mcqs.why: Dry runs reveal logic errors — wrong conditions, missing cases and infinite loops — before coding, when fixes are cheap, and confirm the expected output for known inputs.

mcqs.q: In a dry run of pseudocode, how are variable values tracked?
options: By updating a trace table of variable values as each written step is read in order
By running the code on a computer
By drawing a new flowchart for each step
By guessing the final values first
mcqs.why: With pseudocode, you read each written step in order, updating a trace table of variable values as you go, without running anything on a computer.

mcqs.q: An algorithm that passes dry runs on varied sample data is what, according to the notes?
options: Guaranteed to need no testing ever again
Proven to be the fastest algorithm possible
Far more likely to be correct when finally coded
Ready to be drawn as a flowchart only
mcqs.why: The notes conclude that an algorithm passing dry runs on varied sample data is far more likely to be correct when finally coded, because its logic has already been checked by hand.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes: Learning with LARP
lessons.notes_html:
LARP and its importance

LARP stands for Logic of Algorithm for Resolution of Problems: a fun, interactive way to learn algorithms by actually running them and seeing the results, rather than only reading about them. Learners might physically act out an algorithm — for example, students standing in a line and swapping places to perform a sorting algorithm, or moving tokens along a flowchart drawn on the floor. Its importance is that it makes abstract logic concrete: learners feel why each step happens, see where an algorithm goes wrong, and remember the process far better than from a textbook description. It also builds confidence, because learners experience success in executing an algorithm themselves before they are asked to write code for it, and it encourages teamwork and discussion about alternative solutions.

LARP in practice: improving an algorithm

LARP enhances computational thinking because acting out an algorithm forces learners to use all four pillars at once: they decompose the task into physical steps, recognize patterns in repeated actions, abstract away irrelevant detail (focusing on the rule, not the props), and follow a precise algorithm. Scenario: a class learning to sort exam marks. Students each hold a number card and physically perform a bubble-sort: compare neighbours, swap if out of order, repeat passes until sorted. While acting it out, they notice a pattern — after each pass, the largest remaining number has 'bubbled' to its final place — and they improve the algorithm by stopping each next pass one position earlier, since that part is already sorted. This optimization, discovered through physical experience, is then written back into the pseudocode and flowchart. LARP thus turns abstract principles into lived experience and produces genuinely better algorithms.

mcqs.q: What does LARP stand for?
options: Learning Algorithms by Reading Pages
Logic of Algorithm for Resolution of Problems
Logical Acting for Real Programmers
List of Algorithms and Related Processes
mcqs.why: LARP stands for Logic of Algorithm for Resolution of Problems: a fun, interactive way to learn algorithms by actually running them and seeing the results.

mcqs.q: Which classroom activity is an example of LARP given in the notes?
options: Students standing in a line and swapping places to perform a sorting algorithm
Students copying a flowchart from the board
Students reading an algorithm silently
Students memorising the steps of bubble sort
mcqs.why: Learners might physically act out an algorithm — for example, students standing in a line and swapping places to perform a sorting algorithm, or moving tokens along a flowchart drawn on the floor.

mcqs.q: Why is LARP important for learning algorithms?
options: It lets learners skip understanding each step
It replaces the need to ever write code
It is mainly a way to entertain the class
It makes abstract logic concrete: learners feel why each step happens and see where an algorithm goes wrong
mcqs.why: LARP makes abstract logic concrete: learners feel why each step happens, see where an algorithm goes wrong, and remember the process far better than from a textbook description.

mcqs.q: How does LARP build learners' confidence?
options: By giving them the answers before they try
By letting them watch the teacher perform every step
Learners experience success in executing an algorithm themselves before they are asked to write code for it
By removing all difficult steps from algorithms
mcqs.why: LARP builds confidence because learners experience success in executing an algorithm themselves before they are asked to write code for it, and it encourages teamwork and discussion.

mcqs.q: Acting out an algorithm in LARP forces learners to use what?
options: Only decomposition and coding
All four pillars of computational thinking at once
Only pattern recognition
Memorisation and repetition only
mcqs.why: Acting out an algorithm forces learners to use all four pillars at once: decompose the task into physical steps, recognize patterns, abstract away irrelevant detail, and follow a precise algorithm.

mcqs.q: In the bubble-sort LARP scenario, what pattern do students notice after each pass?
options: The smallest number moves to the front first
All numbers become equal
The order never changes after a pass
The largest remaining number has 'bubbled' to its final place
mcqs.why: While acting out bubble sort, students notice that after each pass, the largest remaining number has 'bubbled' to its final place at the end of the line.

mcqs.q: How do students improve the bubble-sort algorithm through LARP?
options: By stopping each next pass one position earlier, since that part is already sorted
By comparing every pair of numbers twice
By removing the comparison step
By sorting in reverse order instead
mcqs.why: Because the largest number is already in place after each pass, students improve the algorithm by stopping each next pass one position earlier, since that part is already sorted.

mcqs.q: In LARP, abstraction means focusing on what?
options: The props used in the activity
The rule, not the props
The other students in the line
The classroom rather than the algorithm
mcqs.why: The notes say learners abstract away irrelevant detail in LARP by focusing on the rule, not the props, while they decompose, spot patterns and follow the algorithm.

mcqs.q: Where is the improvement discovered through LARP written back to?
options: Only into the students' notebooks
Into the textbook's next edition
Into the pseudocode and flowchart
It is not recorded anywhere
mcqs.why: The optimization discovered through physical experience is written back into the pseudocode and flowchart, so LARP produces genuinely better algorithms, not just better understanding.

mcqs.q: In the LARP scenario for sorting exam marks, what does each student hold?
options: A number card
A printed flowchart
A list of exam questions
A token for a floor diagram only
mcqs.why: In the scenario, students each hold a number card and physically perform a bubble sort: compare neighbours, swap if out of order, and repeat passes until sorted.

lessons.title: Two Questions as Printed: Honest Notes
lessons.notes_html:
The tag question (MCQ 1) as printed

As printed, this question has no correct option, because all four options are correct HTML tags: <div> is a block container, <span> is an inline container, <head> holds a page's metadata (title, links, scripts), and <footer> marks a page or section footer. None of them is incorrect. A student answering this question should note the error in the book rather than guess: if the intended distractor was a made-up tag, it is not present among the options given.

The JavaScript comments question (MCQ 7) as printed

As printed, this question has no single correct option: options (a) and (d) are identical (/* */), and both /* */ (multi-line comments) and // (single-line comments) are valid JavaScript comment markers. Option (c) <-- is not a JavaScript comment (it resembles an HTML comment opening). So the valid JavaScript comment forms among the options are /* */ and //; the question's duplicated option makes a single intended answer impossible, and a student should note this rather than treat one of them as uniquely correct.

lessons.title: HTML Basics
lessons.notes_html:
The <head> tag and page metadata

The <head> tag holds metadata about the web page — information that is not displayed as page content but that the browser needs. It contains the page title (shown on the browser tab), links to external CSS files, internal styles, scripts, and character-set declarations. Everything the visitor reads appears in the <body>, while the <head> prepares the page behind the scenes.

Ordered and unordered lists

An ordered list, created with <ol>, shows items in a numbered sequence (1, 2, 3...), used when order matters, such as steps in a recipe. An unordered list, created with <ul>, shows items with bullet points instead of numbers, used when order does not matter, such as a shopping list. In both cases each item is written inside an <li> tag.

Hyperlinks: the anchor tag

A hyperlink is created with the anchor tag <a> and its href attribute, which holds the destination address: <a href='https://www.example.com'>Visit Example</a>. The text between the opening and closing tags is the clickable link text. The href can point to another website, another page on the same site, or a section within the same page (using an id, such as href='#section1').

The <div> tag

The <div> tag is a block-level container that groups other HTML elements together so they can be styled or positioned as one section — for example, grouping a heading, a paragraph and an image into a 'header' or 'article' block. It has no meaning or appearance by itself; its purpose is structural, letting CSS target the whole group at once.

The <table> tag

The <table> tag creates a table for displaying data in rows and columns. Inside it, <tr> defines each row, <th> defines header cells (bold, centred headings), and <td> defines ordinary data cells. It is used for tabular data such as a marks sheet, a timetable or a price list, and can be styled with CSS for borders, colours and spacing.

mcqs.q: What does the <head> tag hold?
options: Metadata about the web page, which is not displayed as page content
The paragraphs and images visitors read
Only the page's tables and lists
The visible heading at the top of the page
mcqs.why: The <head> tag holds metadata about the web page — information not displayed as page content but needed by the browser, such as the title, CSS links, scripts and character-set declarations.

mcqs.q: Where is the page title set in <head> shown?

Inside the first paragraph
In the address bar only
On the browser tab

mcqs.q: Which tag creates an ordered list?

<li>
<ol>
<order>

mcqs.q: How are the items of an unordered list shown?

Without any marker at all

mcqs.q: In both ordered and unordered lists, each item is written inside which tag?
options: <li>
<item>

mcqs.why: In both list types each item is written inside an <li> tag; <ol> and <ul> only decide whether the items are numbered or bulleted.

mcqs.q: In a hyperlink, what does the href attribute hold?
options: The colour of the link
The text shown for the link

options: Another website

An email address
A section within the same page
mcqs.why: The href can point to another website, another page on the same site, or a section within the same page using an id, such as href='#section1'.

mcqs.q: What is the <div> tag?
options: A tag that displays a horizontal line
A block-level container that groups other HTML elements together
A tag for creating hyperlinks
A table header cell
mcqs.why: The <div> tag is a block-level container that groups other elements together so they can be styled or positioned as one section; it has no meaning or appearance by itself.

mcqs.q: In an HTML table, what does the <th> tag define?

lessons.title: CSS and JavaScript Basics
lessons.notes_html:
Comments in CSS

A CSS comment is written between /* and */ markers, for example: /* This styles the main heading */. Comments are ignored by the browser, so they are used to explain the stylesheet to other developers or to temporarily disable a rule while testing, without deleting it.

Three ways to apply CSS

There are three ways. Inline CSS applies a style directly to one element using the style attribute, for example <p style='color: blue;'>. Internal (embedded) CSS places rules inside a <style> element in the document's <head>, applying to that page only. External CSS places rules in a separate .css file linked from the <head> with <link>, so many pages can share one stylesheet; this is the preferred method for real websites because one file change updates every page.

Including JavaScript in an HTML file

JavaScript can be included in two ways. Internal JavaScript is written inside a <script> element in the HTML document, usually before the closing </body> tag. External JavaScript is stored in a separate .js file and linked with <script src='script.js'></script>. The external method is preferred for larger sites, since the same script can be reused on many pages and kept separate from the page content.

Linking an external CSS file

An external CSS file is linked from the document's <head> using the <link> element: <link rel='stylesheet' href='styles.css'>. The rel attribute says the linked file is a stylesheet, and href gives the file's path. Once linked, every CSS rule in that file applies to the page, and the same file can be linked from many pages.

The CSS box model

The CSS box model describes how every HTML element is treated as a rectangular box made of four layers, from inside out: the content (the actual text or image), the padding (space between the content and the border), the border (the edge around the padding), and the margin (space outside the border separating the element from its neighbours). The total space an element occupies is the sum of all four layers, so setting width, padding, border and margin together determines the element's real size and spacing on the page.
